name: Intent lost between person and code
problem: What someone meant when they asked for a capability lives in their head, a chat or a task, and the code that answers it carries little of that meaning. Months later it is hard for anyone, human or AI, to tell what a module was for, which use cases it must serve, or what "better" would mean for it.
who_has_it: The person who set the direction (Joshua, a Director), the developers and AI agents who change the code later, and anyone deciding whether a part is still needed.
why_it_matters: Code drifts from its purpose, work is redone, and judging a change usually means reading the implementation, which does not scale with AI writing most of the code.
why_hard: Words only approximate intent, intent changes over time, and many agents with no memory between sessions change the code faster than any document is kept current.
existing_attempts: Product requirement documents, architecture decision records, issue trackers, CLAUDE.md files and playbooks, code comments. They hold intent as prose that is rarely checked against the code.

name: Best alternative unknown
problem: Most parts of a system can be done several ways (a model tier, a router, a retrieval method), and the one in use was chosen by whoever wrote it, not by evidence. When a better alternative appears, the evidence that it is better is seldom gathered, and making it the default is a manual change someone has to remember.
who_has_it: Maintainers and AI agents choosing or changing an implementation; Joshua, who wants the best implementation used automatically.
why_it_matters: Quality and cost depend on these choices. Real examples found once measured: a model priced at the wrong rate, a router kept although a cheaper one scored as well.
why_hard: Model output is noisy, costs swing with caching, good test cases are expensive to write, live runs cost money, and "best" differs per use case.
existing_attempts: Ad hoc evaluation scripts, public benchmarks, eval tools (promptfoo, OpenAI Evals, LangSmith), A/B testing platforms, experiment trackers. They measure, but do not tie the result to which implementation runs.

name: Switching means editing code
problem: Switching a provider, runner or backend means finding and editing the call sites, often an `if` chain, and an embedding system cannot switch without forking.
who_has_it: Developers, operators configuring a deployment, and systems that embed a library built on this structure.
why_it_matters: Measuring an alternative is pointless if adopting it is risky and slow, so a measured winner often does not ship.
why_hard: Implementations need different configuration and optional dependencies, and a typo in a name must fail loudly rather than fall back silently.
existing_attempts: Dependency-injection containers, plugin entry points, feature-flag services, factory functions.

name: Metric measures a stand-in
problem: A metric scores a scripted judge, a mocked model or a canned answer instead of the real thing, so its number measures the plumbing around the thing and not the thing. A scripted judge that passes everything scores perfectly, and a decision built on the number has no evidence about the real thing behind it.
who_has_it: Anyone choosing between alternatives by a metric, and the people who review the metric instead of the implementations.
why_it_matters: Review by metric only works if the metric is real; a stand-in number looks like evidence and sends a person to adopt, or keep, the wrong implementation.
why_hard: A stand-in is the easy way to make a model-backed metric cheap, fast and repeatable, and a scripted run does test something real (the plumbing), so the number looks respectable.
existing_attempts: Declaring the arm SIMULATED so the harness does not rank it as paid; unit tests of the plumbing. Neither stops a stand-in from being a solution's only metric.
